post_text:
A patient safety organisation asked a chatbot whether it was acceptable to place a surgical electrode over a patient's shoulder blade.

The chatbot said yes. The organisation says that advice could burn the patient.

That same organisation puts chatbot misuse at the top of its annual health technology hazard list. Its experts say the tools have invented body parts and suggested wrong diagnoses while sounding like an expert.

Here is what bothers me. They are not wrong in a hesitant tone. They are wrong in the same confident tone as when they are right.

Researchers analysed 11,000 real health conversations. Patients ask nothing like the exam-style questions these models are tested on. They ask things that are emotional, leading, sometimes risky.

In one case, someone asked how to do a medical procedure at home. The chatbot told them not to, then gave step-by-step instructions anyway.

I use AI tools. I would still take its diagnosis with a grain of salt.

Where do you draw your line?

#ArtificialIntelligence #DigitalHealth #TechEthics #PatientSafety

claims.claim: A patient safety organisation asked a chatbot whether it was acceptable to place a surgical electrode over a patient's shoulder blade.
claims.evidence: ECRI, an independent, nonpartisan patient safety organization. [...] one chatbot gave dangerous advice when ECRI asked whether it would be acceptable to place an electrosurgical return electrode over the patient’s shoulder blade.

claims.claim: The chatbot said yes.
claims.evidence: The chatbot incorrectly stated that placement was appropriate

claims.claim: The organisation says that advice could burn the patient.
claims.evidence: advice that, if followed, would leave the patient at risk of burns.

claims.claim: That same organisation puts chatbot misuse at the top of its annual health technology hazard list.
claims.evidence: Misuse of AI chatbots in healthcare top the 2026 list of the most significant health technology hazards. The report is prepared annually by ECRI

claims.claim: Experts at the organisation say the tools have invented body parts and suggested wrong diagnoses while sounding like an expert.
claims.evidence: ECRI experts say that chatbots have suggested incorrect diagnoses, recommended unnecessary testing, promoted subpar medical supplies, and even invented body parts in response to medical questions while sounding like a trusted expert.

claims.claim: Chatbots are wrong in the same confident tone as when they are right.
claims.evidence: They are programmed to sound confident and to always provide an answer to satisfy the user, even when the answer isn’t reliable.

claims.claim: Researchers analysed 11,000 real health conversations.
claims.evidence: HealthChat-11K, a dataset of 11,000 real-world health-related conversations... They analyzed these interactions

claims.claim: Patients ask nothing like the exam-style questions these models are tested on.
claims.evidence: They found that the way patients ask questions looks nothing like the way these models were evaluated. Most large language models (LLMs) — the technology underlying chatbots — are tested on exam-style questions
